problem: talking points for a difficult client call
intro: Deliver bad news to a client early, in one plain sentence after a short greeting. Then give one reason you can stand behind, and name the next step with an owner and a date. Write those parts as talking points before you dial. Keep the notes on your Mac, out of the client's view.
tldr: Say the news in your first full sentence, after a short greeting.
Write the news, one reason and the next step as talking points before you dial.
Pick a reply for anger, silence and money requests before the call starts.

blocks.text: Why the first minute decides a bad news call

Clients rarely remember every line of a call. They remember how the bad news landed in the first minute. If you open with small talk about the last project, the client spends that minute guessing. Guessing feels worse than hearing the news. Say the news in your first full sentence. Keep the greeting short. Then stop and let the client react. This is not cold. A busy client wants the point, and a clear start shows you respect their time.

Most people expect hard talks to go worse than they do. In a study led by Kardas, Kumar and Epley in 2021, about 1,800 participants were randomly assigned to deeper or typical conversations. People overestimated how awkward the deeper talks would be. They also underestimated how happy they would feel afterward, according to a Chicago Booth Review summary. The summary is secondhand, so read the figures as reported. The practical lesson is simple. Plan for the call you will probably have, not the worst version in your head.
How to write talking points for a difficult call

Write the talking points on one page, in plain words. Start with the news itself, in a full sentence. For example: The launch moves to the end of next month. Then give one reason you can stand behind. Finish with the next step, with a name and a date if you have them. Keep each line short enough to say in one breath. If a line needs a second breath, cut it.

Here is a worked example. You lead a data project for a retail client. The vendor delivered a model late, and the client's reporting team is waiting. Your talking points could sound like this. The model is late. The vendor missed its agreed date, and we are pressing them for a firm delivery day. We will confirm the new date by Friday. We would like a short call on Tuesday to review the impact. Notice what is missing. There is no list of apologies and no guess about the vendor's motives.

Order matters more than wording. News first, reason second, next step last. If you lead with the reason, the client hears an excuse before the facts. If you skip the next step, the client leaves with a problem and no plan. A clear next step turns a bad call into a planned one. Write the order down so you can glance at it mid-call.
Where to keep notes during a client call on Mac

Keep the talking points where your eyes can reach them but the client cannot see them. Notes on Mac is a good place for this. Apple's Notes guide covers Quick Note, checklists, tags and Smart Folders. Use a checklist for the order of your points. Tag the note with the client's name so you can find it fast. Reading word for word sounds stiff on a call. Use the list as a map, not a script.

If the call runs on Zoom, decide before you join what the client will see. Share one window, not your whole desktop, and only when you need to. Close the notes window before you share a screen. A bad news call is the worst place to show a private draft by accident.
How to tighten a hard sentence with Writing Tools

Some sentences come out defensive or vague on the first try. Apple's Writing Tools can help on your Mac. Select the text, Control-click it, then choose Writing Tools. Rewrite offers Friendly, Professional and Concise tones. Proofread checks spelling and grammar. Run the tool on one sentence at a time, then read the result out loud.

Be careful with rewrites. A tool that softens the news can blur it. If the client ends the call unsure whether the date moved, the rewrite failed. Check that the news is still plain. Apple's guide also says Apple Intelligence is not available in all languages or regions, and usage limits may apply.
How to handle anger, silence and money requests

Clients react in a few common ways. Some get angry. Some go quiet. Some ask for a discount or a refund. Plan one short reply for each reaction before the call. For anger, say you understand the frustration, then stop talking. For silence, wait. Silence is often the client thinking, not refusing. For a money request, say what you can offer and what you cannot, and say you will confirm it in writing.

Avoid promises you cannot keep on the call. Do not guarantee a fix date your team has not agreed. Do not offer a discount just to end the tension. Say you will check, then check. A calm follow-up beats a rushed yes.
Do if-then plans and rehearsal help a difficult call?

An if-then plan links a situation to a response. For example: If the client goes quiet, then you wait for them to speak. The evidence for these plans is real but not perfect. Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) reviewed 94 tests and found a medium-to-large positive effect on reaching goals, with an effect size of 0.65. A later analysis suggests the true effect may be smaller. Treat the if-then habit as a useful tool, not a guarantee.

Rehearsal is less proven. No primary study checked whether rehearsing a hard talk lowers anxiety or improves the result. One secondary source even suggests rehearsal can raise anxiety for some people. So rehearse the first sentence out loud, a few times, then stop. Do not script every word.
Common mistakes when delivering bad news to clients

items: Opening with a long apology. A single clear apology lands better.
Blaming the vendor or your own team in front of the client.
Explaining the reasons before the news arrives.
Promising a date nobody on your team has confirmed.
Reading the talking points word for word.
Ending the call with no owner and no date for the next step.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from the same urge. You want the client to like you again, quickly. That urge is human. It also makes the news harder to hear. Deliver the news steadily first, then warm up the tone after it lands.
Price, scope and deadline news need extra care

Money news has its own rhythm. If the price is going up, say the new number in your first breath. A client hears a number before they hear an apology. If scope is shrinking, name what is out, what stays, and how the timeline changes. If a deadline is moving, say the new date and the reason it moved. Vague timelines create the next difficult call.
What to do after the call

Send a written summary the same day. Write what was agreed, who owns each step, and the date for the next check. Draft it in Outlook while the call is fresh. Read it aloud once before you send. Spoken checks catch the sentences that sound cold on paper.

If the news changes a deliverable, update the affected slides in PowerPoint right away. Add a short note in the speaker notes so the rest of your team sees the change. Clients notice when the deck and the call disagree.

blocks.title: Check client data rules first
blocks.text: Before you paste client names, figures or contract terms into any AI tool, check your employer's rules on client data. Some firms restrict it. If yours does, write the talking points with placeholders, such as [client] and [date], then fill them in by hand.

Questions to answer before you dial

items: What is the news, in a single plain sentence?
What is the reason you can stand behind?
What is the next step, who owns it, and when?
What will you say if the client gets angry or goes quiet?

blocks.text: If you can answer every question in writing, you are ready for the call. If you cannot, fill the gap first. A short delay to the call is better than a vague call.

faq.question: How do I start a call when I have bad news for a client?
faq.answer: Start with the news in one plain sentence after a short greeting. Skip small talk about the weather or the last project. Then give one reason and the next step. Stop and let the client react before you say more.

faq.question: Should I deliver bad news by email or by phone?
faq.answer: For news that changes a date, a scope or a fee, call first. Follow up in writing so you both have the same facts. An email alone can read colder than you meant, especially on a hard topic. Check your firm's norms for this kind of message.

faq.question: What if the client asks a question I cannot answer?
faq.answer: Say you do not know yet, and say when you will know. Write the question down so it does not slip. Only promise a time your team has agreed to. A specific, honest answer beats a guess that changes next week.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur to draft the talking points?
faq.answer: Yes. You can ask Lazur to draft a first version by voice, and it can type text for you. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about something on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. You still choose the reason, the date and the wording. Check the draft against your employer's client data rules.

faq.question: Do I need the talking points on paper during the call?
faq.answer: No. A paper page or a Notes checklist both work. What matters is that you can say the first sentence without reading it. Rehearse that sentence out loud before the call starts.

faq.question: Does rehearsing make a hard call easier?
faq.answer: The research on this is thin. No primary study checked whether rehearsing a hard talk lowers anxiety. One secondary source suggests rehearsal can raise anxiety for some people. Rehearse the first sentence, not the whole call, and watch how you feel.

faq.question: Is it okay to use an AI tool to prepare for a client call?
faq.answer: That depends on your employer's rules, and some firms restrict client data. Check the rules before you paste client names, figures or contract terms into any tool. If you are not sure, use placeholders and fill in the details by hand.

costs.title: Trust after the call
costs.text: A client who hears bad news clearly can still trust you. A client who hears it through fog starts to doubt the next update too. Every vague answer on a hard call creates a question later, often in writing. The cost shows up on the next status call, when the client asks for the same thing again.

costs.title: Your evenings
costs.text: A hard call you dread can take hours of thinking before and after. Most of that time goes to rewriting the same paragraph, rehearsing in your head and drafting a follow-up that should have been easy. Good talking points cut that loop short, because you decide the words once.

costs.title: Scope and fee disputes
costs.text: Unclear bad news invites renegotiation. If the client does not understand the new date or the reason for it, they may ask for a discount to cover the wait. They may also push extra scope into the next phase for free. A clear next step makes those requests harder to justify.

costs.title: Your team's trust
costs.text: Your team feels the call too. If you blame them in front of the client, they lose trust in you. They also stop raising risks early, which means you hear about the next problem later and with less time to act.

causes.title: You expect the call to go badly
causes.text: Your brain forecasts the worst version of the talk, and that forecast makes you delay. A Leadership IQ survey of 689 HR leaders about managers, reported by Forbes, found that 67% of managers regularly avoid or delay critical feedback. The survey year was not stated. The pattern is common enough that putting a hard call off does not make you unusual.

causes.title: The news feels like a personal failure
causes.text: Bad news feels personal, even when the cause sits with a vendor or a changed plan. An HBR headline from 2016 said two-thirds of managers are uncomfortable communicating with employees. The page does not state its sample size, so treat that figure as a headline, not a measurement. Discomfort is common. It does mean you need a script.

causes.title: You have not chosen the reason yet
causes.text: A vague reason invites follow-up questions. If you are not sure why the news happened, you fill the silence with guesses. Those guesses sound like excuses. Settle on the one reason you can defend before you dial. If the reason is still unclear, say that plainly and promise a time to explain.

causes.title: The next step is missing
causes.text: Many bad news calls end with a line like let's talk soon. That line leaves the client holding the problem. Without a named owner and a date, the next call becomes another difficult call. Decide who does what, and when, before you start. Then say it out loud before you hang up.

causes.title: Prep happens too late
causes.text: Many people prepare the work but not the conversation. They open the call with half-formed sentences and hope the words will come. Under pressure, people reach for the first excuse that sounds reasonable. Writing the news and the next step down the night before, or in the morning, prevents that.

fixes.title: Say the news in your first full sentence
fixes.text: Open after the greeting with the news in plain words. Use a sentence the client can repeat to a colleague. For example: The launch moves to the end of next month. Hold the context until the news has landed. You do not need a script for this. You need one clear sentence written before the call.

fixes.title: Give one reason, not a list of excuses
fixes.text: A short, true reason builds trust. A long list of reasons sounds like you are hiding behind them. Pick the reason you can defend in a follow-up question. If you cannot defend it, do not use it. Say you are still confirming the cause, and say when you will know.

fixes.title: Name the next step, owner and date
fixes.text: End the news part with the next step. Say who owns it and the date you will check in. If you do not have a date yet, say when you will have one. A next step gives the client something to hold. It also gives you a test you can pass after the call.

fixes.title: Write the talking points in Notes, then tighten them
fixes.text: Build a checklist in Notes with the news, the reason, the next step, and replies for anger and silence. Use Writing Tools to tighten one sentence at a time. After each rewrite, check that the sentence still says the news plainly. Keep the final version short enough to scan in a glance.

fixes.title: Use an if-then line for the reaction you fear most
fixes.text: Write one line in the form: If the client does this, then you do that. Put it in your notes, and keep it simple. Research on implementation intentions is encouraging, though the effect may be smaller than early studies suggested. Test the habit on a low-stakes call before you rely on it in a hard one.

fixes.title: Send the written summary the same day
fixes.text: Put what was agreed in writing within the same day. Include the news, the reason, the owner of each step, and the next date. A written summary gives the client something to forward and something to check against. Read it aloud once before you send it.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Write the news in one sentence
plan.text: Open your draft client thread and write the news in a single plain sentence. Add the reason you can stand behind and the next step. If you cannot write that sentence yet, you are not ready for the call.

plan.label: Before the call
plan.title: Build the talking points in Notes
plan.text: Create a checklist in Notes with the news, the reason, the next step, and a reply for anger, silence and money requests. Tag the note with the client name so you can find it during the call.

plan.label: Before the call
plan.title: Rehearse the first sentence aloud
plan.text: Say the first sentence out loud a few times, then stop. Add an if-then line for the reaction you fear most. Keep it short enough to recall under pressure.

plan.label: During the call
plan.title: Stop and let the client react
plan.text: After the news, pause. Let the client speak first. Answer the question they ask, not the one you prepared for. If you do not know, say so, and say when you will know.

plan.label: Same day
plan.title: Send the written summary
plan.text: Draft the follow-up in Outlook while the call is fresh. Include what was agreed, who owns each step, and the date for the next check. Read it aloud once before you send.

plan.label: Next week
plan.title: Review how the news landed
plan.text: Check the client's next message. Did the questions change? Did the next status call go more smoothly? Write a line in your notes about what to say next time.
